title: Complex Analysis for Physicists
subject: Complex Analysis
summary: Complex numbers and functions, analyticity, contour integration, Laurent series and the residue theorem, with the physics payoffs: real integrals, Fourier and Laplace inversion, causality and Kramers-Kronig, conformal maps for 2D potential flow and electrostatics, and saddle-point ideas behind Stirling. Chemistry hooks: AC impedance, response functions, dispersion relations in spectroscopy.

units.title: Complex Numbers and Elementary Functions
units.summary: Algebra and geometry of the complex plane, Euler's formula, roots, multivalued logarithms, and why complex exponentials are the physicist's tool for oscillations and impedance.

lessons.title: Complex Arithmetic and Euler's Formula
objectives: Perform addition, multiplication, division and conjugation of complex numbers in Cartesian and polar form and interpret each as a geometric operation.
Derive Euler's formula from the power series of exp, cos and sin.

lessons.title: de Moivre's Theorem, Roots and Trigonometric Identities
objectives: Use de Moivre's theorem to compute powers and to find all n-th roots of a complex number, plotting them as vertices of a regular polygon.
Derive trigonometric identities (multiple-angle, product-to-sum) by expanding exp(i n theta).

lessons.title: Complex Exponential and Trigonometric Functions and the Logarithm
objectives: Write exp, sin, cos, sinh and cosh of a complex argument in terms of real functions and verify standard identities.
Define the complex logarithm ln z = ln r + i(theta + 2 pi k) and explain its multivaluedness and the principal branch.

lessons.title: Complex Powers, Inverse Trigonometric Functions and Branch Points
objectives: Evaluate complex powers z^a = exp(a ln z) and inverse trigonometric functions such as arcsin 2.
Locate branch points of simple functions (sqrt z, ln z, sqrt of (z^2 - 1)) and describe a branch cut.
Explain how the multivaluedness is seen by walking once around a branch point.

lessons.title: Complex Series and Disks of Convergence
objectives: Find the radius and disk of convergence of a complex power series and relate it to the nearest singularity.
Sum geometric series in the complex plane, e.g. sum of cos(n theta) via Re sum e^{in theta}.

lessons.title: Phasors, Impedance and Nyquist Plots
objectives: Use phasors to solve a driven RLC steady state, defining the complex impedance Z = R + i(omega L - 1/(omega C)).
Connect to chemistry: impedance spectroscopy and Nyquist plots in electrochemistry are plots of Z in the complex plane.
demoIdeas: Nyquist-plot builder: assemble R, L, C in series/parallel and see Z(omega) traced in the complex plane.

units.title: Analytic Functions and Conformal Mapping
units.summary: Complex differentiability, the Cauchy-Riemann equations, harmonic functions, and conformal maps for 2D electrostatics and fluid flow.

lessons.title: Complex Functions as Maps and the Cauchy-Riemann Equations
objectives: Regard f(z) as a map from the plane to the plane and describe the image of simple regions under z^2, 1/z and e^z.
Derive the Cauchy-Riemann equations from the requirement that the limit defining f'(z) is independent of direction.
demoIdeas: Pick f(z): see a polar grid mapped to its image; angles preserved wherever f' is nonzero.

lessons.title: Testing Analyticity and Harmonic Conjugates
objectives: Test whether a given function is analytic and find its derivative, and explain why z-bar and |z|^2 are not.
Find the harmonic conjugate v of a harmonic u and construct the analytic function f = u + iv.
State that the real and imaginary parts of an analytic function satisfy Laplace's equation, linking to electrostatics and steady flow.
demoIdeas: Pick u(x,y): draw the level curves of u and of its harmonic conjugate v on one plot and see them cross at right angles; swap in non-analytic choices like |z|^2 or Re z and watch the orthogonality fail.

lessons.title: Conformal Maps and Mobius Transformations
objectives: Show that an analytic map with f' != 0 preserves angles and scales lengths locally by |f'|.
Use the linear fractional (Mobius) transformations, w = (az + b)/(cz + d), to map circles/lines to circles/lines.

lectures.title: Topic 10 notes: Conformal Transformations (conformal maps and Mobius transformations)

demoIdeas: Apply a Mobius map to a grid of circles and lines and watch them stay circles and lines.

lessons.title: Conformal Maps for Laplace Problems and Complex Potentials
objectives: Solve a 2D Laplace problem by mapping a complicated region to a simple one, such as a half-plane or the unit disk.
Interpret an analytic function as a complex potential for 2D electrostatics or ideal fluid flow, with equipotentials and stream/field lines as orthogonal families.

Topic 10 notes: Conformal Transformations (mapping regions and solving Laplace problems)

units.title: Cauchy's Theorem, Integral Formula and Series
units.summary: Integration in the complex plane and its remarkable consequences: path independence, derivatives of all orders, and Taylor and Laurent expansions.

lessons.title: Contour Integrals by Parametrisation and the ML Inequality
objectives: Parametrise a contour and evaluate integral of f(z) dz directly for circles, line segments and arcs.
Use the ML-inequality to bound a contour integral.
demoIdeas: Drag the shape of a path between two fixed points (line, arc, wiggle) and read the numerical integral of z^2 and of conj(z): the first is path independent, the second changes with the path.

lessons.title: Cauchy's Theorem and Contour Deformation
objectives: State Cauchy's theorem and explain it as the Green/Stokes theorem plus the Cauchy-Riemann equations.
Show that integral over a circle of z^n dz is 2 pi i for n = -1 and zero otherwise, and explain the pole as the source of nonzero values.
Deform a contour freely across analytic regions and handle a region with holes by multiple contours.
demoIdeas: Contour deformation: drag a closed curve over a plane with colored singularities; integral value updates and jumps by 2 pi i when crossing a pole.

lessons.title: Cauchy's Integral Formula and Its Derivative Form
objectives: State and apply Cauchy's integral formula f(a) = (1/2 pi i) oint f(z)/(z - a) dz and its derivative version.
Use it to evaluate integrals such as oint e^z/(z - a)^n dz.

lessons.title: Analytic Functions Are Power Series: Liouville and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
objectives: Prove that an analytic function has derivatives of all orders and is locally a convergent power series.
State Liouville's theorem and the maximum-modulus principle, and give the fundamental theorem of algebra as a corollary.

lessons.title: Taylor Series and Laurent Expansions in Annuli
objectives: Expand a function in a Taylor series about an analytic point and find its radius of convergence from the nearest singularity.
Compute Laurent expansions in different annuli for a rational function such as 1/(z(z - 1)) using geometric series and partial fractions.

lessons.title: Classifying Isolated Singularities and the Residue
objectives: Classify an isolated singularity as removable, a pole of order m or essential from its Laurent series.
Explain why the coefficient of 1/(z - a) is called the residue, using integration of the Laurent series term by term.

units.title: Residues and Real Integrals
units.summary: The residue theorem as a machine for evaluating contour integrals and, by closing contours, definite integrals of real functions.

lessons.title: The Residue Theorem and Simple Poles
objectives: State the residue theorem and derive it from Cauchy's theorem by shrinking small circles around the poles.
Compute the residue at a simple pole as lim (z - a) f(z), or p(a)/q'(a) for f = p/q.

lessons.title: The Sokhotski-Plemelj Formula and the i-epsilon Prescription
objectives: Derive the Sokhotski-Plemelj formula $1/(x-a\pm i\epsilon)=\mathrm{P}/(x-a)\mp i\pi\delta(x-a)$ by displacing the pole above or below the real axis.
Explain the $i\epsilon$ prescription in physics: the sign of $\epsilon$ encodes causality, and the formula evaluates integrals such as $\int f(x)/(x-a+i\epsilon)\,dx$.

units.title: Physics Applications and Extensions (Grad Touch)
units.summary: The point at infinity, the argument principle, inversion of transforms, Kramers-Kronig dispersion relations and the saddle-point method behind Stirling's formula.

lessons.title: The Point at Infinity and Residues at Infinity
objectives: Compute the residue at infinity and use it to evaluate an integral by summing the residues outside a contour.
Verify by the substitution $w=1/z$ that the finite residues and the residue at infinity sum to zero, and decide when the point at infinity gives the shortest route to an integral.

lessons.title: The Argument Principle and Stability
objectives: State the argument principle: the winding of f along a contour equals the number of zeros minus the number of poles inside.
Use the argument principle to count the zeros of a polynomial in a region.
Relate stability analysis (zeros of the characteristic polynomial in the right half-plane, Nyquist criterion) to winding numbers.

lessons.title: Inverse Laplace Transforms and Poles as Resonances
objectives: Invert a Laplace transform with the Bromwich integral by closing to the left and summing residues at the poles.
Describe how a pole's position in the complex plane gives the resonance frequency and the width (lifetime) of an excitation.

lessons.title: Causality and the Kramers-Kronig Relations

Derive the Kramers-Kronig relations connecting the real and imaginary parts of a causal response function from Cauchy's integral formula.
Interpret them for a spectroscopic response: the refractive index (dispersion) and absorption coefficient of a material are Kramers-Kronig pairs.
